items.readable_text:
Content:
The kernel of a linear transformation is the set of vectors that map to the zero vector. We define it formally as follows:

Content:
> For a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}], the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is the set of all the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{u}] such that [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.] We can write this as
> [MATH: \textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) = \left\{ \;\mathbf{u} \;| \; \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0} \right\}.]

Content:
The diagram below shows the kernel of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}: V \rightarrow V] in a vector space [MATH: V].

Notice that, because of linearity, the zero vector is always in the kernel of a linear transformation:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{T}(0\cdot\mathbf{v})=0\cdot\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=0]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the linear transformation [MATH: [x; y]] and the vectors [MATH: [2; 1]] Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A vector [MATH: \mathbf{u}] belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] if [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.]

Therefore, we need to compute [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_i)] for each vector [MATH: \mathbf v_i\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: T(v_{1})|= T([2; 1]) = [0; 0]; T(v_{2})|= T([3; 1]) = [2; − 3]; T(v_{3})|= T([2; 3]) = [− 8; 12]]

Since [MATH: \,\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)=\mathbf{0},] we conclude that, of the given vectors, the only vector that belongs to the kernel of [MATH: \,\mathbf{T}] is [MATH: \,\mathbf{v}_1.]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the linear transformation [MATH: [x; y; z]] and the vector [MATH: [k; 2; 6]] Find the value of [MATH: \,k\,] such that [MATH: \,\mathbf{u}\in\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A vector [MATH: \mathbf{u}] belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] if [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.]

So, we need to solve the following equation:

[MATH: T(u)|= 0; [3 ⋅ k + 12 ⋅ 2 − 3 ⋅ 6; − 2 ⋅ k + 4 ⋅ 2 − 2 ⋅ 6; 6 ⋅ k − 3 ⋅ 2 + 3 ⋅ 6]|= [0; 0; 0]; [3k + 6; − 2k − 4; 6k + 12]|= [0; 0; 0]]

Therefore, we get the system [MATH: {3k + 6 = 0; − 2k − 4 = 0; 6k + 12 = 0.]

The solution to all three of these equations is [MATH: k=-2.]

We know how to determine whether a given vector is in the kernel of a linear transformation. But how do we find the kernel of a linear transformation?

Content:
First, remember that if [MATH: T] is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T},] then
[MATH: \textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{Null}(T) = \left\{ \;\mathbf{x} \;|\; T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0} \right\}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Finding the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}.]

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is [MATH: [2|4; 3|6]]

Setting [MATH: [x; y]] we then need to solve the equation [MATH: T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.] First, we reduce [MATH: T] to row echelon form, as follows:

[MATH: T|= [2|4; 3|6]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− (3)/(2))R_{1}; ∼[2|4; 0|0]]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is [MATH: x,] and we have one free variable, [MATH: y.] That means we need to find [MATH: x] in terms of [MATH: y.]

From the first equation, we get [MATH: x=-2y.]

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation [MATH: \,\mathbf{T}] is [MATH: [− 2y; y]]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we write down the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [2|4|0; 4|10|− 1; − 6|− 12|1]]

Recall that [MATH: \textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{nullity}(T) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)).]

In order to find [MATH: \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)),] we reduce [MATH: T] to row echelon form, as follows:

[MATH: T|= [2|4|0; 4|10|− 1; − 6|− 12|1]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 2)R_{1}; ∼[2|4|0; 0|2|− 1; − 6|− 12|1]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + 3R_{1}; ∼[2|4|0; 0|2|− 1; 0|0|1]]

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot columns. Therefore, [MATH: \textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T))=0.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The kernel of a linear transformation is the set of vectors that map to the zero vector. We define it formally as follows:

Content:
> For a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}], the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is the set of all the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{u}] such that [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.] We can write this as
> [MATH: \textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) = \left\{ \;\mathbf{u} \;| \; \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0} \right\}.]

Content:
The diagram below shows the kernel of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}: V \rightarrow V] in a vector space [MATH: V].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/440e63deccaf707e7d4cd12fc39b5db5]

Content:
Notice that, because of linearity, the zero vector is always in the kernel of a linear transformation:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{T}(0\cdot\mathbf{v})=0\cdot\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=0]

Content:
for any vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}].

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

Example Prompt:
Consider the linear transformation
[MATH: [x; y]]
and the vectors
[MATH: [2; 1]]
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A vector [MATH: \mathbf{u}] belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] if [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.]

Therefore, we need to compute [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_i)] for each vector [MATH: \mathbf v_i\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: T(v_{1})|= T([2; 1]) = [0; 0]; T(v_{2})|= T([3; 1]) = [2; − 3]; T(v_{3})|= T([2; 3]) = [− 8; 12]]

Since [MATH: \,\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)=\mathbf{0},] we conclude that, of the given vectors, the only vector that belongs to the kernel of [MATH: \,\mathbf{T}] is [MATH: \,\mathbf{v}_1.]

---

Item 5 — Example: Calculating a Component of a Vector in the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

Example Prompt:
Consider the linear transformation [MATH: [x; y; z]] and the vector [MATH: [k; 2; 6]] Find the value of [MATH: \,k\,] such that [MATH: \,\mathbf{u}\in\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A vector [MATH: \mathbf{u}] belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] if [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.]

So, we need to solve the following equation:

[MATH: T(u)|= 0; [3 ⋅ k + 12 ⋅ 2 − 3 ⋅ 6; − 2 ⋅ k + 4 ⋅ 2 − 2 ⋅ 6; 6 ⋅ k − 3 ⋅ 2 + 3 ⋅ 6]|= [0; 0; 0]; [3k + 6; − 2k − 4; 6k + 12]|= [0; 0; 0]]

Therefore, we get the system
[MATH: {3k + 6 = 0; − 2k − 4 = 0; 6k + 12 = 0.]

The solution to all three of these equations is [MATH: k=-2.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

Content:
We know how to determine whether a given vector is in the kernel of a linear transformation. But how do we find the kernel of a linear transformation?

Content:
First, remember that if [MATH: T] is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T},] then
[MATH: \textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{Null}(T) = \left\{ \;\mathbf{x} \;|\; T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0} \right\}.]

Content:
Therefore, to find all the vectors in the kernel of a linear transformation, we just need to find the null space of the corresponding standard matrix. We can do this by solving the matrix equation [MATH: T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

---

Item 9 — Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

Example Prompt:
Consider the linear transformation [MATH: [x; y]] Find [MATH: \textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T}).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Finding the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}.]

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is [MATH: [2|4; 3|6]]

Setting [MATH: [x; y]] we then need to solve the equation [MATH: T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.] First, we reduce [MATH: T] to row echelon form, as follows:

[MATH: T|= [2|4; 3|6]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− (3)/(2))R_{1}; ∼[2|4; 0|0]]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is [MATH: x,] and we have one free variable, [MATH: y.] That means we need to find [MATH: x] in terms of [MATH: y.]

From the first equation, we get [MATH: x=-2y.]

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation [MATH: \,\mathbf{T}] is [MATH: [− 2y; y]]

Item 12 — Tutorial: The Nullity of a Linear Transformation

Content:
The nullity of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is the dimension of its kernel. This means that
[MATH: \text{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = \dim(\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T})) = \text{nullity}(T).]

Content:
To compute the dimension of the kernel of [MATH: \mathbf{T},] we just have to reduce the matrix [MATH: T] to row echelon form and count the number of non-pivot columns.

---
